mappings.note: Aligning and then displacing the three pierced matchboxes and looking for the light spot: an investigation whose result shows light travelling straight.
Removes the screen, then the object, then changes the object's colour and records what happens to the shadow each time: a systematic set of trials.
Looks at a flame through a straight pipe and then a bent one: the straight-line test run in another form.
Sorts a list of materials into transparent, translucent and opaque by how much light each passes: classification by a property.
Draws the conclusions of the shadow activity, including what the size of the shadow depends on: inference from the trials just made.
States the three things a shadow needs: source, obstruction and screen. The conditions of the phenomenon explained, not an experiment run.
A shadow stays dark whatever the object's colour because it is a region light does not reach: the nature of a shadow explained.
Asks for the conclusion of the pinhole observations: an inference drawn from what was seen.
The inverted flame on the screen of the pinhole camera, explained by rays crossing at the hole: reading the working of a device built in class.
Whether the pinhole images are coloured and upside down: further properties of the same constructed device.
Picks the luminous objects out of a list that mixes stars, planets, the Moon and a mirror: classification by whether the object makes its own light.
Records what is seen when a pen is held before a plane mirror: the first observation of the mirror activity.
Compares image size with object size across positions, another recorded observation from the same activity.
Checks whether the image stays upright as the pen is moved: the orientation observation of the activity.
Tries and fails to catch the mirror image on a screen, which is the test that shows the image is virtual.
Moves closer and notes that the image moves in too, establishing the equal-distance relation by observation.
Whether a Z-shaped tube can serve as a periscope and where the mirrors must go: designing and explaining a working device from available materials.
A high-flying bird casts no visible shadow but a swooping one does: the observation traced to how much light is blocked at that distance.

Fireflies and the purpose of the light they make: a light-producing organism recognised by that feature. No outcome in this frame covers animal communication, so identification is the closest honest home.
The Moon placed as non-luminous because it only reflects sunlight: classification by source of light.
Names the luminous class.
Names the non-luminous class, the companion category.
Matches pinhole camera, opaque object, transparent object and shadow to their descriptions: sorting the chapter's categories.
Only the observer in line with the openings sees the flame, because light travels in straight lines: the outcome traced to that cause.
Picks the picture whose shadow falls on the correct side of the boy, relating shadow direction to where the light is.
Ball near the torch against ball near the wall: shadow size related to the positions.
Matches each change in the set-up, closer torch, farther torch, object removed, second torch, to its effect on the shadow.
Asks for the pinhole image of the tree to be sketched, so the assessed act is drawing. Not LO-155, because the camera's working is assumed rather than explained.
Sketch the mirror image of your written name (LO-153) and then explain the lateral inversion behind the difference (LO-150). Both are asked for.
The shadow is shortest at noon because the Sun is highest then: the measured pattern traced to its cause.
Judges two statements about lateral inversion and about letters that look unchanged: the property of the mirror image explained.
Names the opaque class for materials that stop light completely.
Predicts no light spot behind cardboard, which follows from placing cardboard in the opaque class.
How a shadow forms, by an object blocking the path of light: the phenomenon explained.
The three requirements for a shadow, the one-mark version of the same explanation.
Darker shadows from opaque objects against fainter ones from translucent objects: two classes of material set against each other, which is LO-146 rather than the sorting of LO-147.
Moving the object towards the source enlarges the shadow: the change tied to its cause.
Moving the object towards the screen shrinks the shadow, the companion cause-and-effect item.
Picks lightning as the natural source among manufactured ones: classification of light sources.

LED lamps promoted because they draw far less power and last longer, which is about not consuming resources needlessly. Cited at competency level because LO-158 lists pollutants, tree planting and sanitation, none of which covers energy saving.
